narr: Low pressure began organizing in the Gulf of Mexico on the 16th, setting record low sea level pressures as it traversed the Southeast through the 17th. Strong high pressure over the North Atlantic created a deep southeasterly flow that drew warm air into New England ahead of the approaching storm. By the time precipitation arrived on the evening of the 17th, temperatures were warm enough for rain everywhere except the highest peaks. Early on the 18th a shortwave trough was approaching from the Great Lakes and led to rapid deepening of the low pressure as it paralleled the Eastern Seaboard. Even as the center of the storm remained near Chesapeake Bay on the morning of the 18th, a strong low level jet had developed and winds began to gust in excess of 50 mph well inland from the coast. Damaging wind gusts continued into the afternoon. Thousands of customers lost power due to falling limbs and downed wires. The anomalously warm air mass also led to intense rainfall rates beginning on the evening of the 17th, which continued into the 18th. Upsloping winds also enhanced precipitation along the southeast facing slopes of the White Mountains. Widespread 3 to 4 inches of rain fell, with isolated pockets of 6 to 8 inches. This fell on top of snow that was ripe from previous rainfall about a week earlier. An additional 2 to 3 inches of snow water equivalent was likely added to rainfall runoff. Numerous road washouts and road closures occurred due to flash flooding and fast responding small stream and tributaries. Localized moderate to major flooding occurred along mainstem rivers with the majority of New Hampshire Rivers outside of the mountains only reaching minor flood stage.
ev: Heavy rain and rapid snowmelt combined with steep terrain to produce rapid runoff. The resulting runoff over frozen ground caused NH-116 from Paine Road to NH-112 in Easton to close due to flash flooding from Judd Brook.

Rapid runoff from Bear Mountain caused Clark Brook to flood portions of Bristol to Hebron to Alexandria, including Gove Road. King Road after Burns Hill Road was washed out caused by excessive run-off from higher terrain in the region.

Heavy rain and rapid snowmelt combined with steep terrain to produce rapid runoff. The resulting runoff over frozen ground caused NH-25 at Elijah Beede Road and Elijah Craig Road in Sandwich to be closed due to flooding from the Meadow Brook.

Heavy rain and rapid snowmelt combined with steep terrain to produce rapid runoff. The resulting runoff over frozen ground cause numerous washouts and sinkholes along Route 302, along with a rockslide near Willey House. All lanes were closed from mile 43.6 to 55.8 in Crawford Notch.

Heavy rain and rapid snowmelt combined with steep terrain to produce rapid runoff. The resulting runoff over frozen ground caused numerous washouts and sinkholes along the Kancamagus Highway/NH Route 112. Flooding from the adjacent Swift River also eroded a 100 foot section just west of Conway.

Heavy rain and rapid snowmelt combined with steep terrain to produce rapid runoff. The resulting runoff over frozen ground caused flooding from the Rocky Branch River in Glen New Hampshire. The Stilling's Road became inundated and was closed due to the flooding.

Heavy rain and rapid snowmelt combined with steep terrain to produce rapid runoff into the Ellis River. The small stream became a raging river after 6 inches of rain and 3 inches of snowmelt overwhelmed the stream system. Downstream in Jackson, properties along the river were inundated, along with several roads being damaged. The main thruway, NH Route 16, closed at mile marker 92.6, and adjacent NH 16B also flooded. Washouts were also reported in many local roads like Green Hill Road.

Heavy rain and rapid snowmelt produced around 9 inches of combined runoff. All small streams in the Presidential Range region exceeded their banks. This was true in Jefferson, New Hampshire where numerous small streams flooded Route 115 and Route 2, causing these roads to be closed.

Major flooding of the Moose River with an estimated rain and snowmelt between 8 and 9 inches of liquid runoff. The resultant flow was estimated around 6500 CFS, which is greater than the 0.2% annual exceedance level, or 500 year flood. The river overflowed its banks surrounding homes and flooding basements off Bellevue Place near the Gorham Airport. Additional flooding occurred on Water Street and Broadway Avenue. Flood waters topped the Route 2 bridge shutting down a major throughway in the region.

Major flooding of the Moose Brook with an estimated rain and snowmelt between 8 and 9 inches in runoff. The resultant flow is estimated over a 0.2% recurrence interval with flows between 3 and 4 kcfs. The most severe damages were near Pike Industries in Gorham, which suffered a washed-out bridge and floodwaters compromised a building. The nearby storage facility was inundated with unknown damages. Jimtown Road flooded but no reported homes where damaged. The flows overwhelmed the Moose Brook bridge overtopping onto Route 2. A large truck was picked up by the flood waters and wedged under the bridge, along with significant amounts of rocks and debris.

Heavy rain and rapid snowmelt combined with steep terrain to produce rapid runoff. The resulting runoff over frozen ground caused flash flooding on the Ammonoosuc River causing a closure of the Tunnel Brook Bridge in Easton.

Significant damage occurred on the Peabody River on December 18th following a heavy rain and rapid snowmelt event. The USGS river gage in Gorham went from under 100 cfs around midnight, to over 13,000 cfs by noon. The streamflows were estimated to be around the 1% annual exceedance or 100-year flood level. Rainfall amounts where estimated around 5 inches with an additional 3 inches of rapid snowmelt runoff. The ground conditions were frozen, supporting complete runoff. One home off Route 16 was deemed unlivable and a complete loss after floodwaters eroded the foundation. Property was also damaged at Great Glen Trails Outdoor Center near the headwaters. Downstream in Gorham the damage was most prevalent along Bell Street and after the confluence with the Androscoggin River. Major damage occurred downstream to the town of Shelburne.

Heavy rain and rapid snowmelt combined with hilly terrain to produce rapid runoff. The resulting runoff over frozen ground caused washouts on Stokes, George, Braley and Butternut Ridge Roads in Hebron. North Shore Road from Gray Rocks Road to Cross Road flooded by the Cockermouth River. The Cockermouth River crested at 9.75 based on the USGS river gage located upstream of Hebron. This was 1.5 feet less than that reached following Irene in 2011.
